blocks.content: This topic pulls together everything from this module and the last into one practical checklist: the concrete techniques that take a bloated image and make it small, fast to pull, and quicker to build.

Applied together, a small base image, multi-stage builds, and a lean build context routinely take a naive Dockerfile's multi-gigabyte image down to well under a hundred megabytes, a difference that matters for pull times, storage costs, and attack surface all at once.

blocks.alt: The combined effect of every technique in this module

blocks.content: Each separate RUN is its own layer, chaining related steps with && into one instruction avoids leaving behind intermediate layers that only add size without adding anything useful to the final image.

blocks.alt: One chained instruction instead of several small ones

blocks.content: 3. Clean Up Within the Same Layer
blocks.text: 3. Clean Up Within the Same Layer

blocks.content: Deleting a package manager's cache in a separate, later RUN instruction does not actually shrink the image, that data is still sitting in an earlier layer. Cleanup has to happen in the same RUN instruction as the install, so it never gets committed to a layer in the first place.

blocks.alt: Cleanup only helps if it happens in the same layer as the install

blocks.content:
# Wrong: cache is already committed to a layer, this RUN does not help
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl
RUN rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# Right: cleanup happens before the layer is committed
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

blocks.content: The single highest-leverage technique for compiled languages remains multi-stage builds, keep every compiler and build tool confined to a builder stage that never ships, and copy across only the finished artifact.

blocks.alt: The build toolchain never has to reach the shipped image

blocks.content: 5. A Real Tradeoff to Be Aware Of
blocks.text: 5. A Real Tradeoff to Be Aware Of

blocks.content: Optimization is not purely "fewer layers is always better," fewer, larger combined layers can actually reduce cache granularity, a small change might now invalidate a bigger combined layer than it would have invalidated as several smaller ones. Balancing final image size against cache-friendliness is a judgment call, not a fixed rule.

blocks.alt: Combining layers trades some cache granularity for a smaller image

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: Combining RUN instructions, cleaning up within the same layer as the install, and using multi-stage builds together deliver the biggest size wins.
Optimization is a tradeoff, not a checklist to maximize blindly, fewer combined layers can mean coarser cache invalidation.
